[P3] 出版者的话

古希腊圣哲亚里士多德曾说：“任何人都会生气，这没什么难的，但若要适时适所地以适当方式对适当对象恰如其分地生气，可就难上加难了。”而我们现在讲的情绪管理指的就是要适时适所地对适当对象恰如其分地表达情绪。

现实生活中，人们越来越多地认识到情绪管理能力的重要性，因为这方面能力出众的人往往在各个领域都游刃有余；相反，此项能力差的人，虽然可能很聪明，但做起事来往往很吃力。

情绪管理能力虽部分得益于先天因素，但归根结底还得靠后天的学习和培养，而幼儿时期是情绪管理能力培养的黄金时期。一个人在幼儿时期所获得的情绪经验和习惯会在大脑中形成永久的神经联结，对其身心发展影响很长远。

当前，亲子共读情绪管理类图画书这种情绪管理能力培养方式已被广泛认可。优质的图画书好比幸福的种子，通过父母的声音飞进孩子的耳朵里，植根在孩子的心底，施以阳光、雨露就能生根、发芽。

这套有趣的动物图画故事书温情脉脉，每一本都是有针对性地就孩子的某一种情绪话题展开，描绘孩子的心路历程，揭示其走出情绪困扰并解决问题的过程。每一本书都附有幼教专家精心撰写的导读，可作为家长亲子共读时的参考。

让我们在这套书的陪伴下，去享受一段美妙的亲子阅读之旅吧！

[P4] 老师对你说
林中的小世界
这是一本充满生活气息的图画书，讲述了小松鼠罗宾与几位邻居的故事。文中一开始说到罗宾“刚刚搬到新家，在一片新的树林中心的新的树上”，作者连续用了几个新字，提示读者小松鼠新生活的开始。
小松鼠把院子收拾得好整洁啊！还铺上了漂亮的桌布。接下来他会做什么呢？他出门了。从眼神中就能够感觉出，他的心里充满了渴望，但还有些担心和犹豫。不过为了结识更多的新朋友，他还是勇敢地敲开了邻居猫头鹰的家门。然而他的满脸笑容换来的却是猫头鹰的不信任。接下来遇到的是啄木鸟的怀疑、小刺猬的惊恐，还有凶巴巴的小兔子。他们的冷漠和疏远与小松鼠罗宾的热情、大方、真诚形成了强烈的反差。最后，当邻居们遇到困难的时候，小松鼠不计前嫌，挺身而出，无私地帮助大家，终于换来了信任和尊重。
故事除了表现邻里之间互相帮助的意思外，还有更深刻的含意，那就是让孩子懂得拒绝与被拒绝。现实生活中每个孩子都有过这样的经历：想玩同伴的玩具，被拒绝；想和同伴一起游戏，被拒绝。如何正确认识并接受拒绝，是孩子在社会交往中不可避免的

[P5] 题。作为父母或老师，我们一方面要引导孩子以平常心来看待被拒绝，坦然接受，使孩子懂得别人有权利拒绝他；另一方面，我们也要让孩子学会反思，想一想自己为什么会被拒绝，怎样做才不会被拒绝。故事中的小松鼠罗宾之所以被拒绝，是因为他在拜访朋友的时候选择了不适当的时间，打扰了猫头鹰和小刺猬的休息，而啄木鸟正在忙着啄树干，小兔子在忙着打洞，大家是不愿意在这时被打扰的。还有，如果罗宾能够直接表达自己的意愿，告诉邻居们，自己是想请他们到家里做客，大家也许会好好考虑的。

我们还可以借着这个故事让孩子们学会换位思考，如果自己不想去做某一件事，可以拒绝别人，但是一定要给出对方能接受的理由，不至于让对方难过。例如，故事中的邻居们可以对罗宾说，他们现在有事，过一会儿再找他。

小松鼠的邻居们可以毫不掩饰地拒绝，也可以在刚刚拒绝别人后又反过来寻求帮助，转瞬之间冰释前嫌，这才是孩子们的世界吧！没有记恨，简单纯洁得让人爱怜。这也时刻提醒我们不能从成人的角度去评判孩子们之间的矛盾冲突，而要认真地倾听和引导，这样才能帮助孩子逐步养成良好的交往习惯。

（保定市教科所教研员 刘育红）

“早上好！我叫罗宾，你的新邻居！”

[P22] 原来，猫头鹰、啄木鸟、小刺猬和小兔子都来了。
他们提着一个装得满满的篮子。
小兔子说：“我们弄了一些柴火。”
小刺猬接着说：“为了冬天取暖用。”
啄木鸟无助地说：“但是，篮子卡住了。”
猫头鹰最后发言，他说：“我们就没办法把篮子带走了。”

“是啊！”小兔子说。
“帮帮我们吧！”小刺猬也点点头。
“我们很需要……”啄木鸟说道。
“你的帮助！”猫头鹰最后总结。

[P27] “嗨！”“呦！”

[P29] “工作过后，我们需要休息一会儿。”小伙伴们都说。
于是小松鼠提出建议：
“一起去我家吧，尝尝我们松鼠的特色美食，怎么样？”
四个小伙伴你看看我，我看看你，都脸红了。

[P30] 小兔子最先对小松鼠说：“对不起。”
接着，小刺猬低声说：“我们做错了。”
啄木鸟也红着脸说：“那时，我们还不认识你。”
猫头鹰最后说：“所以我们有点儿担心。”
小松鼠微笑着说：“没关系，没关系，
现在你们认识我了，都请来我家吧！”

[P33] 于是，猫头鹰、啄木鸟、小刺猬和小兔子都来到小松鼠家，

小松鼠罗宾笑着回答：“就是想邀请你们来我家吃小吃呀！”

[P3] Publisher's Note

The ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle once said: 'Everyone gets angry, and that's not difficult. But to be angry at the right time, in the right place, in the right way, and with the right person, to the right degree—that's difficult indeed.' What we now call emotional management is precisely about expressing emotions appropriately, at the right time and place, toward the right person, and to the right extent.

In real life, people are increasingly recognizing the importance of emotional management skills, because those who excel in this area often thrive in various fields; conversely, those who lack this ability, although perhaps very intelligent, often struggle in their endeavors.

While emotional management skills may partly stem from innate factors, they ultimately depend on learning and cultivation in later life. Early childhood is the golden period for developing emotional management skills. The emotional experiences and habits formed during this period create permanent neural connections in the brain, profoundly influencing a person's physical and mental development.

Currently, the method of cultivating emotional management skills through parent-child reading of emotional management picture books is widely recognized. High-quality picture books are like seeds of happiness, carried into children's ears by parents' voices, taking root in their hearts, and with sunlight and rain, they can grow and flourish.

This series of heartwarming animal picture storybooks is designed to address specific emotional topics for children, illustrating their inner journeys and revealing how they overcome emotional challenges and solve problems. Each book includes a carefully written guide by early childhood education experts, serving as a reference for parents during parent-child reading.

Let us enjoy a wonderful parent-child reading journey together with this series!

[P4] Teacher Says to You
A Little World in the Forest
This is a picture book full of life, telling the story of little squirrel Robin and his neighbors. At the beginning of the story, Robin is described as having 'just moved into a new home, on a new tree in the center of a new forest,' and the author uses several new words to signal the start of Robin's new life.
Robin tidies up his yard so neatly! He even lays out a beautiful tablecloth. What will he do next? He goes out. From his eyes, you can sense his longing, but also some worry and hesitation. However, to make more new friends, he bravely knocks on the door of his neighbor, the owl. But his cheerful smile is met with the owl's distrust. Next come the woodpecker's suspicion, the hedgehog's fear, and the grumpy little rabbit. Their coldness and distance form a strong contrast with Robin's warmth, generosity, and sincerity. Finally, when the neighbors face difficulties, Robin, without holding grudges, steps forward and selflessly helps everyone, eventually earning their trust and respect.
Besides showing the meaning of mutual help among neighbors, the story has a deeper message: to help children understand rejection and being rejected. In real life, every child has had such experiences: wanting to play with a peer's toy and being refused; wanting to play with a peer and being refused. How to correctly understand and accept rejection is an unavoidable part of children's social interactions.

The growth treasure trove of playful and explorative Songta Beibei

[P5] Topic. As parents or teachers, on one hand, we should guide children to view being rejected with a calm mind, accept it calmly, and help them understand that others have the right to reject them; on the other hand, we should also help children reflect, think about why they were rejected, and how to avoid being rejected. The reason why the little squirrel Robin was rejected in the story is that he chose an inappropriate time to visit his friends, disturbing the owl and the hedgehog's rest, while the woodpecker was busy pecking the tree trunk and the little rabbit was busy digging a hole. Everyone was unwilling to be disturbed at that time. Also, if Robin could directly express his intention and tell his neighbors that he wanted to invite them to his home as guests, they might have thought about it carefully.

We can also use this story to help children learn to think from others' perspectives. If one doesn't want to do something, they can reject others, but they must give a reason that the other person can accept, so as not to make the other person sad. For example, the neighbors in the story could tell Robin that they are busy now and will look for him later.

The neighbors of the little squirrel can reject others openly, and they can also seek help from others right after rejecting them, resolving conflicts instantly—this is truly the world of children! Without grudges, simple and pure, it is endearing. This also constantly reminds us not to judge conflicts among children from an adult's perspective, but to listen and guide them carefully, so that we can help children gradually develop good social habits.

(Baoding City Educational Research Institute, Researcher Liu Yuhong)

[P7] Once upon a time, there was a brown little squirrel whose name was Robin.
He had just moved to a new home,
On a new tree in the center of a new forest.

[P9] To make more new friends,
Robin decided to visit the small animals in the forest.

[P10] First, Robin knocked on the owl's door.
"Good morning! I'm Robin, your new neighbor!"
But the owl said distrustfully:
"But I've never seen you in the forest!"
Robin said:
"I just moved here, and I have some things I'd like to ask you."
"I'm not interested!" the owl said coldly.
Then, the owl closed the door, continued sleeping, and waited for night to come.

[P13] Next, Robin knocked on the woodpecker's door.
"Good morning! I'm Robin, your new neighbor!"
But the woodpecker said suspiciously:
"But I've never seen you in the forest before!"
Robin said:
"I just moved here, and I have some things I'd like to ask you."
"I'm not interested!" the woodpecker said coldly.
Then, the woodpecker closed the door and continued "thumping" the tree trunk.

[P15] Then, Robin knocked on the hedgehog's door.
"Good morning! I'm Robin, your new neighbor!"
But the hedgehog said nervously:
"But I've never seen you in the forest!"
Robin said:
"I just moved here, and I have some things I'd like to ask you."
"I'm not interested!" the hedgehog said coldly.
Then, the hedgehog closed the door and continued curling up to sleep.

[P17] Finally, Robin knocked on the little rabbit's door.
"Good morning! I'm Robin, your new neighbor!"
But the little rabbit said grumpily:
"But I've never seen you in the forest!"
Robin said:
"I just moved here, and I have some things I want to ask you."
"I'm not interested!" the little rabbit said coldly.
Then, the little rabbit closed the door and continued digging in its own burrow.

[P19] Robin had no choice but to return to the tall oak tree,
back to his little nest.

[P20] After a while, the little squirrel heard an unusual sound.
Then, he climbed out of his little nest.
Next, he was stunned by what he saw.
18

[P22] Originally, the owl, woodpecker, hedgehog, and little rabbit had all come.
They were carrying a basket full to the brim.
The little rabbit said, "We gathered some firewood."
The hedgehog continued, "For keeping warm in winter."
The woodpecker said helplessly, "But the basket is stuck."
The owl spoke last, saying, "Then we just can't take the basket away."

[P25] "Perhaps, I can help you," Robin suggested.
"Yes!" said the little rabbit.
"Help us, please!" the little hedgehog nodded.
"We really need..." the woodpecker said.
"Your help!" the owl concluded.

[P27] "Hi!" "Oh!"
The little squirrel jumped up and down, very agile,
and in no time reached the branches that were blocking the basket.
He skillfully pushed the branches aside,
and the basket could be taken out again!
The four friends were very happy and thanked the little squirrel for his help.

[P29] "After working, we need to rest for a while," the friends all said.
Then the little squirrel made a suggestion:
"Let's go to my house and try our squirrels' special delicacies, how about it?"
The four friends looked at each other, blushing.
They suddenly remembered the scene earlier that morning when they had turned Robin away.

[P30] The little rabbit spoke to the little squirrel first: "I'm sorry."
Then, the little hedgehog whispered: "We were wrong."
The woodpecker, blushing, said: "At that time, we didn't know you yet."
The owl said last: "So we were a bit worried."
The little squirrel smiled and said: "It's okay, it's okay,
now that you know me, please all come to my house!"

[P33] So, the owl, woodpecker, hedgehog, and little rabbit all came to the squirrel's house,
and together they ate roasted pine nuts and sugar-fried hazelnuts.
They were overjoyed!

[P34] "By the way, Robin, what did you come to ask us this morning?"
The owl remembered Robin's visit earlier in the day.
The little squirrel Robin smiled and replied, "I just wanted to invite you all to my house for some snacks!"

[P35] From then on,
the group of inseparable friends in the forest added a new member,
and they often played together and helped each other under the oak tree.

[P2] 本页为绘本《树林里的小松鼠罗宾》的扉页，展示了书名、作者、插画师、译者及出版社信息，画面中有一只小松鼠和三只小动物（兔子、猫头鹰、小鸟）在奔跑，右下角有二维码及推广文字。
